utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I only notice the absence of Mr. Meek, who I suppose has spent a sleepless night pondering on my -- and is now taking a well-earned rest. Yes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Mr. Meek will not be with us today and at the beginning of next week. He's expected to arrive on Thursday next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I must have complicated his mind. It needs a rest. Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls for the Prosecution. I can't see anyone else behind the column. All right. I understand there is a preliminary, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. It's a very short matter I wish to raise before the witness begins, and I continue with my cross-examination. This is an issue that arose over the weekend when I spoke with the Prosecution and I asked them a question arising from the second interview which was provided by the witness on 17th of March 2002. On that occasion, the witness provided a lot of new information that was not provided before, and this happened or was triggered by a question which was put to him and the following question is the -- this one. It says that: "Further to that, we learned that a request had been made to your battalion to provide people to participate in this execution. Can you tell me about that?" And then at that moment, the witness started to speak and to provide new information. The question I posed to my friends from the Prosecution was where did they get that information in order to help us do our own investigation? So far I have not been able to -- my colleague has not replied to this query. They told me that they are looking for the information as to where -- who provided this information to the Prosecution so that they could put this question to the witness. But so far, I haven't got any answer. And I'll pursue my cross-examination but I thought it was important to inform the Trial Chamber that that's a piece of information that was missing when preparing for this witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if you wish to comment. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We do endeavour, when we get the occasional question like this, to see if we can answer it simply. I was able to answer a similar question and provide an ancient secret source document for the counsel to find out which rumour led to another rumour which led to a question. This one, we are looking for to help him out and we'll continue to look. I don't think the law obligates us to do this but there is no problem us looking and we'll continue to look. The problem is the -- Mr. Bursik's been asked and doesn't recall but we'll continue to look to see if we can sort it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's bring the witness -- I suppose there are no further matters to be raised? Okay. How much time do you think you will require, Mr. Bourgon? You gave us an indication yesterday but I don't know whether you've --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I do have quite a substantial amount of questions and I will try to do my best to finish in two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've just asked you, not curtail your time, but to be able to plan the rest of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point we have probably less than a half hour, if any at all, but we are still waiting to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like also to ask the Chamber to put to the witness some additional questions regarding yesterday disclosed documents from the Prosecution. This is a vehicle work log, just -- I need not more than ten minutes for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll consider that later on. Thank you. Yes, good morning to you, Mr. Acimovic. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am very confident that we will finish today. But please try to keep your answers short as possible, provided they are pertinent to the question, they answer the question, the whole question and nothing but the question. Because otherwise you will be here again next week. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Before I begin with my questions that I had planned to ask you today, I have a couple of clarifications from testimony you gave either yesterday or the day before. Firstly I'd like you to confirm that you would agree with me that you are able to recognise or that you were able to recognise the voice of Drago Nikolic. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And yesterday, I asked you a question concerning the position of Drago Nikolic, and I suggested to you that he was the assistant commander for security and not the assistant commander for intelligence and security. You -- your response was that you weren't aware of that. Now, I'd just like to recall that in your first statement, the first interview, and that was on page 4, and also in English and in B/C/S, you stated that Drago was only chief of security. Do you recall saying that in your first interview?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, a quick clarification also, something you mentioned in your testimony on the 20th of June, so that's two days ago, you mentioned, and that was on the transcript page 23, lines 16 to 17 of that transcript, you mentioned that Trbic was a reserve lieutenant. Now, I suggest to you that in fact Trbic was not a reserve lieutenant but that he was a captain. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when he was promoted, when he became captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also mentioned concerning Trbic that he was a foot soldier in your battalion. Would I be correct in saying that in fact, just before leaving or just before being reassigned to the brigade command, he was your deputy commander? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me clarify, if I may. When I first met Trbic, it was while I was still the company commander. He was a foot soldier then. When I was appointed pursuant to an order of the brigade commander, the commander of the 3rd Infantry Battalion, and since I had known Trbic from before, in agreement with the brigade commander, I appointed Trbic my deputy. This was in 1992, I think. In November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you for this information and clarification. So would I be right in saying that he was your -- or maybe I should put it this way: How long was he your deputy commander, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise answer, but I would say that maybe a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And would I be right in saying that, of course, because he was a your deputy commander and that you even knew him before that, that you were quite close to Trbic? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, we knew each other well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move on, Mr. Acimovic, to my first area of questions for today. And the first thing I'd like to do is simply confirm the sequence of events as you described them and then we'll go into each of those events one by one. But the first thing that took place, I'm talking just in general terms, is when you went to the school with the priest and the president of the local community. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And after spending some time at the school, you were on your way back to your battalion command when you stopped in Kozluk to make a phone call; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Following which, according to your testimony, you returned to the school and you spoke to both the priest and the president of the local community?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I had spoken to the priest. I'm not sure about that. But I did speak to the president of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the next thing that took place is you returned to your -- after speaking to the president of the local community, you returned to battalion command from where you made another phone call to the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the sequence of events, then came the first telegram and the first response which you sent back?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please put your question in a more precise way? Because I'm not sure that I have understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. Acimovic. When you are in -- back at the battalion command, the next event which took place that really -- that you testified about is when you say that you -- that the battalion received a telegram from the brigade and that you forwarded a response back to the brigade. So that's the next major event.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And following which there was a second telegram and a second response; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at some point, because I don't want to be too precise, we'll get to the precise details in a minute, but at some point in this telegram business, you consulted with the company commanders?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could get in touch with company commanders. I was able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. And then the next major event is phone calls that you say were made to you by Drago Nikolic. That would be the next major event?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Let me just clarify my previous answer, please. I said before that I had been in touch with company commanders or their deputies. I know that I spoke to the commander of the 1st Company and as for the 2nd and the 3rd Companies, I don't know whether I spoke to the commanders or their deputies. I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. It is indeed important. But the purpose of my question was there was some consultation at that point with the companies. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No consultations took place. The company commanders were informed about the telegram that we had received. I asked my company commanders whether they were familiar with the telegram, and I suppose that they answered affirmatively, and as I have already stated in my previous statements, I informed them about our reply to these telegrams, and I also informed them on that occasion that if anybody should check, that they should say that they were familiar with the content of the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to the details of what happened with the company commanders or their deputies, as you mentioned. I was just trying to set up the sequence of events. And the next thing that happened was the alleged conversation with Drago Nikolic, and then you went after that in the morning you went to Rocevic where you met with Popovic. Is that in the sequence of events what happened according to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then there was several days later a meeting for battalion commanders at brigade command. That would be the next event you testified about, both in examination-in-chief and when you answered questions from my colleague Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether that was a few days later, I don't know. I can't be sure of that. But I suppose that some time did pass after all of these events that I've -- that we've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a quick clarification before I move on to my next topic. And that is concerning the priest. I take it from your testimony that when you initially went to the school, you met the priest and the president of the local community, we know that, but I'd like to know, is it your -- what is your testimony in terms of how long did the priest stay there with you? Was he there during the consultation process when you tried to get access to the school?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we were given some information by the Prosecution. They managed I guess to meet this priest and according to the information we have, he said that he stayed five minutes and went back to his church. Does that sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I take it, then, that when -- if he only stayed five minutes that means that when you approach those unknown and uncontrolled soldiers who were guarding the school, the priest was not witness of these events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move on to my next topic which is simply I'd like to cover with you some information I think is necessary regarding the communication which your battalion had, both to the companies and to the brigade. So let's begin with between the battalion and the brigade command. Would you agree with me that there was a line -- a land line, meaning telephone hooked from wire -- by wire from telephone to telephone?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's a military telephone where you basically have to turn the telephone and then you get the person at the other end? And would you agree with me that this is --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- that this is a secure line, meaning that conversations on such a telephone cannot be intercepted unless you plug yourself in the wire?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And both at the brigade command and at the company command -- and at the battalion command, sorry, there is a switchboard. You are aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if you called to the brigade, you will first get the switchboard and the switchboard will connect you to any office in the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I move to communications between the battalion command and your own companies, there is also a land line, wire from phone to phone, so basically there is a secure telephone connection between the battalion command and all of your companies?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So these conversations cannot be intercepted, once again, unless someone plugs right into the wire?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as mentioned, there was, in your battalion, a switchboard, and that was a TLC 10. Familiar with that, Mr. Acimovic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you're familiar with the fact that there was a switchboard and that the switchboard was located in the communication section, 40 metres away from the battalion command, is that the case?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So anyone who wants to have access to the battalion must first ring the switchboard and then is connected either to a company or to the battalion command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as for communications between the battalion and the brigade forward command post, the IKM, would I be correct in saying that you did not have a direct line to the IKM, that you must first call brigade command who would then connect you to the brigade IKM?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the line which exists between the brigade command and the brigade forward command post or IKM is also a military secure line, a wire between two phones?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that in addition to this military phone, there was also a radio network on which there was a number of stations which would link the brigade command and all the battalions as well as the brigade IKM?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if the commander of the brigade or the Chief of Staff goes away for -- from the brigade command while remaining in the brigade area, it would be the norm or the normal procedure for the Chief of Staff to bring along a radio?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the Chief of Staff would also carry along or not carry along but usually will be accompanied by a radio operator who would be with the Chief of Staff at all times or very close to him?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my question is not whether it did take place but that's the procedure that should take place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, of course, this radio network which would link the brigade command to the brigade battalions, the radio network, that's -- those conversations can be intercepted if you have a radio device and you can switch on to the right frequency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Unless, of course, you use the device which is the RUP 12, I believe, which would code the communication?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not competent to answer your question. I don't know enough to be able to talk about the communication system, if we are talking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll move on in my questions and simply to add that some battalion commanders had also a Motorola radio?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you yourself have a Motorola radio?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the Motorola radio, can you get from this radio -- can you get on the brigade network?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I never had occasion to speak on the Motorola radio with the commander or the Chief of Staff, because we always had more secure communications, the telephones that we discussed earlier. So it was not necessary to talk on the Motorola. And since the units concerned were static, they were infantry battalions, including mine, that were linked to their own area of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you yourself I take it, then, made very little use of your Motorola, if any?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We probably used it, but very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it that in addition to the military secure line and the radio network, there were in some places civilian phones; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the civilian phones is what you call an open line or an unsecure line?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already that I'm not competent to discuss communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then my question would be -- I'll move on. Thank you, Mr. Acimovic. I have enough for in terms of what I wanted to know to clarify concerning communications and I move to my next topic, which deals with the procedure within the battalion command. And my first question is: There would always be an operative duty officer at the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the operative duty officer is the one who receives and sends all information on behalf of the battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the duty officer has an operational logbook in which he writes all important information that takes place during his shift?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, for example, if you have -- as the battalion commander, are away from your battalion, and someone calls and tries to get ahold of you, the duty officer would write this in the book and say, "Mr. X tried to call the commander at such a time"? Would that be a normal procedure?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe the duty officer kept that kind of record.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what kind of record did he keep? What did you insist that your duty officer keep as record?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer at the battalion command usually received telegrams and he was the communication link with the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we'll get to telegrams later but what if it's not a telegram? What if it's simply someone who wants to speak to the commander of the battalion and you're not there? Where will the duty officer note down the message? In the operational duty book or just on a piece of paper that he will give you when you come back?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know whether that's the kind of message he would note down or he would just tell me, pass it on to me, relying on his memory, or he would perhaps call me by some means of communication, telling me that somebody was trying to get in touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I try to make a comparison between the battalion command duty officer and the brigade command duty officer, would I be right in saying that they have somehow the same duties at different levels, of course?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago, all my assistants were soldiers, so that every shift on duty anybody did, boiled down to receiving information, passing it on to me and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe you didn't understand my question correctly. I'm just looking now at the brigade command duty officer. Would I be right in saying that he would also be the link, he's the one who is the communications link, passing the information to all the battalions? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the brigade duty officer, you know because either you saw it or you know it from experience, that he also has a duty officer logbook?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure there is a logbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you never saw it yourself, the logbook?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we've heard quite a bit of testimony in this case concerning the fact that if there was communication addressed to the brigade duty officer, he did have a book and he did write this down. Would that be a normal procedure, according to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection. Sorry to interrupt. It's just about the terminology. Earlier my friend was referring to a logbook and now it's a book and I think we are all talking about the notebook but I just want to make that -- we have been trying to work out the terminology exactly but I think just for the record that's what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood that. Do you agree, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would agree with the Prosecution, like I always do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead and try to speed up this part, if you can. I think it's been overlaboured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just Mr. Acimovic, the -- if at the battalion command a telegram was received, and you referred to that earlier, it would be noted in the notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, some information has been provided to us by the Prosecution concerning the person you say was on duty that night, Mitar Lazarevic, and in the information we received, it says that there was a separate logbook for telegrams that was beside the phone and that telegrams were immediately registered. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I move on to another section of the cross-examination. Yesterday, in response to a question by my colleague Mr. Zivanovic, you confirmed that you met the Prosecution three times before coming to The Hague for your testimony. That was on page 24, lines 22 to 25. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at page 25, lines 17 to 20 you also confirm that whenever you remembered something new, then in your subsequent statement you would add this to the previous statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through my interviews with the Prosecution, I kept recalling certain things as we went along.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to confirm with you that during your first interview, there are issues that you did not mention to the Prosecution. The first such issue was the first telegram you received asking you to provide a platoon to participate in executions. In the first interview you did not mention that.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that on that occasion I had not been asked such questions. I had not been asked things like that during the first interview, and I did not recall them then. At that time, I was trying to answer the questions that I was asked, and since the events in question took place a long time ago, I hope you will agree with me that seven years on, one cannot recall every detail. Do you perhaps agree with me? Did it ever happen to you that you were going shopping for three things and arriving at the shop you no longer had any idea of what they were? Now, imagine events of a different kind and a time interval of seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Even though I should be the one asking the questions I'll answer to yours and I agree with you. Now, let's just go to what was not mentioned in your first interview and then we can try and address why it was not mentioned. But right now, I think it is important for the Trial Chamber to know exactly what was not in your first interview. So if you can please just answer by yes or no, if you want to elaborate I will never stop you but I think we can move quicker if we just keep to yes or no. The second telegram asking you to provide a platoon to participate in executions, that was not mentioned in the first interview.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The phone calls that you say you received from Drago Nikolic that night and at 7.00 in the morning, that was not mentioned either?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was mentioned concerning the telegrams, nothing that fell under that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So going to the school the following morning and having a meeting with the accused Popovic in Rocevic, that was also not mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I can show you your statement but I'm telling you that it's not in the first interview but I don't want -- if you don't agree we can look at the interview if you want but do you agree that it's not there?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say it's not there, I suppose it's not. But I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then we'll have to look at the interview because it's not my word that counts. It's yours. So unless -- if I may have on e-court -- and I think to make it easier, Mr. President, I can give a copy to the witness in his language, a paper copy. He can just flip through it. It's going to go quicker and save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It has -- you need to show it first to Mr. Nicholls to -- not that I don't trust you but it's for formality's sake and do you agree with that -- with this procedure, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't need to see it. I'm sure it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you agree with the proposition that Mr. Bourgon is putting to the witness in any case, Mr. Nicholls? Because if you do, there is no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There is no need absolutely if my colleague stipulates it's not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I don't want to interfere with his cross but I think the witness has already basically answered when he said that he didn't discuss the telegrams or the phone calls in the first interview and that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, if my colleague says that he agrees that those events are not there because I think I it's important to get precise information. He did not say that he went to the school that day, he did not say that he met the accused Popovic that day. I think it's important to be precise about those details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are prepared to stipulate that, we can move much faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, so we can proceed. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I appreciate the assistance of my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Acimovic, I take it you had the time but we solved the matter now and those events are not mentioned in your first interview. Now, you mentioned earlier, when I asked you, you said that you did not remember these things or that you were not asked. I would just like to refer to you, if you can -- maybe if the witness can keep it and I'll refer him to some questions he was asked on that occasion, I'd like you to look on page 30, Mr. Acimovic, and that's 3D153, and if we can call this up on e-court. In English, the reference is page 31, lines 20 to 25. Now, all I want to refer to you is the three questions that were posed to you during that interview. The first one on page 30 was: Do you know anything about the execution of prisoners in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade? Do you see this question in your language on page 30, Mr. Acimovic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't have the exact line unfortunately. In English, it's 23 to 25 but in your language, it's line 18. If you look at line 18 you will find this question -- 14? Just where it says, "Do you know anything about the execution of prisoners in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you can move, Mr. Acimovic, to page 23? In English, page 24, lines 23 to 25. Do you see the question, Mr. Acimovic, "Did you ever found out what happened to these people?"

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Page 23, and line is close to 21, 22, 23. Question is, "Did you ever found out what happened to these people?" Page 23. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Line 22.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if you can move now, Mr. Acimovic, to page 28? In English the reference is page 19, lines 19 to 25. Now, the question you were asked then was, "Did you get any feedback from either your brigade commander or Popovic about what happened to those people?"

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I look at these three questions, and I compare this to your answer that -- or I simply suggest to you that you really did not remember anything about those telegrams and those phone -- and those telephone conversations because with those questions, you would have remembered, right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall what exactly I remembered at that moment, how much I remembered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, if you could give me the English page number again of the last part? Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I have in my notes here is page 19, lines 19 to 25 but it would seem strange because the 28 in B/C/S so maybe I have-- it's 29, sorry. Maybe that's the problem. Page 29, lines 19 to 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That explains because I was trying to follow on page 19 and I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise. It's page 29, lines 19 to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Acimovic, when you were cross-examined by my colleague, you stated something, and that was on page 31, talking about yesterday, lines 15 to 25. So I'll just read your answer that you provided then and then I'll ask you a question: "My first statement that I provided in Banja Luka was accessible to many people in Zvornik. I did not consider that to be right."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, one moment, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, I forgot to mention in the beginning of the sitting but I am saying it now, with retroactive effect, that we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis today due to Judge Stole being unable to be with us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, I move now to your second interview, and during that second interview, and I think to make that easier I can give you a paper copy also, if my colleague agrees, and I can refer to you some lines that you can see for yourself, that you read I believe, with the Prosecution on Sunday, so it won't be any surprise to you. And for the sake of e-court, this is 3D154. And if we can call the English copy on e-court and I refer you, Mr. Acimovic, to page 7. Now, I just put to you this question -- not put to you, I just ask you to look at this question where it says, "Further to that, we learned that a request had been made to your battalion to provide people to participate in this execution. Can you tell me about that?" Immediately after being asked this question, you provided information concerning the-- what you referred to as the telegrams and the telephone conversations. Now, I suggest to you, Mr. Acimovic, that if you had not been asked this question, you would not have mentioned this information. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from this question -- just a minute. As you can see from the way the question was worded, it gave me a basis for recalling certain events. It helped me remember them. You can see that for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that was exactly my point. I just wanted to know whether you had decided before the interview to provide this information or you suddenly remembered when this question was put to you. Which of the two is it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I think that I remembered at that moment because of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I look at your third interview -- so we can do away with this -- with the second one for now, do you recall that in your third interview your status was changed to that of a suspect?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall that after your status had been changed to that of a suspect, you provided a lot of information concerning Obrenovic which you appear to have refused to provide before you were made into a suspect?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see what I have disclosed to Obrenovic. I just said that I thought he must have known. That's why I thought and said that he was aware of that, but I also said that I couldn't be sure. I just suppose that if he was in the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade, he should at least have known about those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is indeed one of the things you said when your status was changed to that of a suspect. So what you're telling me is even if you had not been made a suspect you would have provided this information, the same information?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's just take three quick examples and maybe we can avoid having you look at the material. I'll just quote from the statement where you said at one point if the duty officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is two pages. I would like the witness to be able to look at the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do not agree, without going into it in front of the witness, with all of my friend's assertions he's just made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's give him the opportunity to go through these two pages first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have a paper copy given to the witness? We do have a copy on e-court but it's not the right version so we cannot use e-court at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to see it, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I believe my colleague has a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have a look at that document -- what's happening, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I gave the wrong paper, I'm sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I will have to quote from it because it's not available in the language of the accused. Sorry, of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. I think it's in e-court in B/C/S. I think we were looking at it yesterday in B/C/S in e-court and we -- I don't have a hard copy in his language but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Registrar, Madam Registrar, if we locate it --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I do have it on paper to give to the witness. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I did as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, witness, you are going to be handed a two-page document which I kindly ask you to go through, please. Can we have the exact number of that document. Is it the right document, Madam Registrar? You don't know?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's actually three pages, Your Honour, but I think the area at issue is two pages. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I think it's better, Mr. President, if I can just read the three little parts I want to read to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We still have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Date of the document is 11 November 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can I speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to have it correct in the record it's 1D002; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's 1D202. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I approach my colleague for one quick minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, if I can refer you to the document you have in your hands in your language, and right at the beginning, if we can go to the first page, or sorry, the second page, where you ask -- the paragraph begins by: "Asked again if he thought Obrenovic was trying to avoid him, Acimovic said that it was not logical that Obrenovic would not have known what was happening as there were military phones, civilian telephones, radios and if all else failed, communication could have been made by means of a courier and that it should have been impossible for him not to know what was happening." Do you have this paragraph, Mr. Acimovic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I refer you now to the next paragraph. That's when you were made a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, but that's not accurate. There is a paragraph in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's the paragraph in between I want to read to him now. I said next paragraph. I was getting to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The paragraph, Mr. Acimovic, reads as follows: "When asked about the identity of the soldiers at the Rocevic school, Acimovic said that he did not know who they were and that they definitely were not from Zvornik Brigade." And then he talks about "... a rumour that Jasikovac and his MPs were at the school but that he had not seen them himself." And that's when you were made into a suspect. Now, after that, after having been made a suspect at that time, you did not provide any other information concerning what happened at the Rocevic school or in terms of the identity of the soldiers at the Rocevic school, did you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see here, I have stated that I did not see Jasikovac in the Rocevic school. I suppose that he arrived once I had already left. When I said that I had heard that he had been there, that means that he probably came after I had already left to rejoin my unit. This is what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You can do away with this document, Mr. Acimovic. My question is simply that everything you said to the Prosecution this Sunday, you did not say on that occasion, despite the fact that you were made a witness [sic]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We just saw, you and I, that you were made a suspect on that occasion, you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you were made a suspect because Mr. McCloskey, my colleague, thought that you were not being honest concerning the identity of the people in Rocevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And despite being made a suspect, you did not provide any of the information at that time which you provided this Sunday?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, at that moment I failed to remember quite a number of things. During each subsequent interview, my memory was additionally jogged about the events that I could not remember previously. I've also said that some details, especially names, I did not mention for the reasons of safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For safety or out of memory? Which of the two? The names. I thought you just mentioned that you did not remember but then you just added that you did not mention the names for reasons of safety. So at that time, you remembered those names or you did not remember these names at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll try to finish with this topic simply by what I need to cover with you is what you told the Prosecution for the first time this Sunday when you met for your proofing session. Now, in this case, I think my colleague will agree we do not have a document in the language of the accused. All we have is an English copy, so I'll just put to you what you mentioned to the Prosecution, and I'd just like you to confirm that you did not mention these things or, sorry, that you mentioned these things for the first time this Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, sorry to interrupt, I just ask my colleague to remember what should be in private and what should not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Acimovic, this Sunday, or -- you mentioned for the first time that the accused Popovic had instructed you to go outside and to find a person in the crowd to take part in the execution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to find a person. Are you referring to a specific person, to somebody concrete?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm referring to the information which was given to me by the Prosecution, which is a list of what you told them. And I will quote from this document. I will use the exact words so that there is no confusion. And I will read exactly what I've been told by the Prosecution. Then you can confirm yes or no. We are not talking about names yet and whenever there is a name we will go into private session to protect these names. Is that okay? The first one is, "Popovic said that someone must be willing to do it and instructed the witness" - you - "to go outside and find persons in the crowd to take part in the execution." That was the first time you mentioned this, this Sunday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was within that context, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The second part is: "One of the soldiers who were guarding the prisoners showed up and said he had found a person who volunteered to take part in the execution." You mentioned this for the first time this Sunday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody showed up. I said one of the soldiers who guarded the prisoners arrived together with that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But my question is you mentioned this for the first time this Sunday.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And a little later, you -- the information you provided is that a soldier came in the office and told Popovic that one truck had arrived from the brigade. This is the first time you mentioned this information to the Prosecution, on Sunday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe we can move in private session just to be sure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Bourgon. Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll say the question again, Mr. Acimovic. Do you remember that during your proofing session with the Prosecution, you were asked the following question: If you had any knowledge that a boy or young man from Rocevic volunteered to take part in the killings of prisoners? Do you remember this question was asked of you on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what I suggest to you, Mr. Acimovic, is that it is this question, and because you were asked this question, that you decided to provide the rest of the information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remembered that answer in my conversation with the Prosecutor. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So all this information you did not remember until you had the conversation with the Prosecution on Sunday, is that your statement or your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you that I only remembered some information in my conversation with the Prosecutor. They were prompted by his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can go back, Mr. President, back in private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that. Let's go back to open session because now it's important -- private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. We will continue with your cross-examination after the break, which will be of 25 minutes' duration. ---. Recess taken at 10.33 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, we'll move on to a different area now. I'd like to come back on your testimony during --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, before we move on to the next subject may I ask for some clarification? On the last two questions, the counsel was putting pressure on me and I gave one hasty answer and I want to be given an occasion to explain what exactly I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, go ahead, Mr. Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One, one moment. Should we be in open or in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If he mentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you going to mention Mitar Lazarevic or are you going to mention other names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some more people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you may proceed with your questions. We are in open session, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, before I proceed with my next question, I just want to make it clear that it is not my intention to mislead you in any way or to play with words, and if at any point you want me to repeat a question, I will repeat this question and give you the time to give your answer. That being said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I could also add, Mr. Bourgon, because this is how I have been educated in conducting trials, that if at any moment any counsel here, be it from the Prosecution or from the Defence, is playing games, we usually intervene to protect the witness. So unless we intervene, you can take it that we do not consider the questions, either specifically or in general, to be an abuse of the process. Okay, so you can rely on us that we will intervene when it's the case of intervening. I can understand that some witnesses feel somewhat irritated with some questions but that doesn't necessarily mean what you say. So, please, rely on us to intervene when it is necessary. I don't think it was the case of intervening at any moment so far. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, my first question, which arises from what you just mentioned, and the opportunity you had to address the Trial Chamber, is that is it your testimony today that you have been withholding this information from both the Prosecution and the Defence investigators that you've met over the past number of years, and that you've had this information from the beginning, or you just remember lately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's answered the question. I think he's answered the question. About names, he had the information all the time. But he took a decision to withhold that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, Mr. Acimovic, is you say that this was a decision you made after giving your first statement which became known. I don't understand why in the first statement you did not give this information?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was also aware, and let me say first that this was not the case solely with my statements. Rumour had it that all the witnesses who give statements are not sufficiently protected in that sense. Information leaks through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, Mr. Acimovic, is that you mentioned that this withholding of names for safety reason, of course it applies to names. And then you mentioned a little earlier on that there was and I quote from page 39, line 8, you say that "It is true that I failed to remember some small details that I consider them minor." My question is the following: Is receiving a telegram asking you to provide a platoon of soldiers to participate in execution, is this something you consider to be a small detail and minor?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that is extremely important.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Acimovic. I move on to my next topic and I will deal now with the events which took place in Rocevic. And my first question is the following: In addition to the information you provided to the Prosecution on Sunday, the new information, it was the first time in your testimony two days ago that you mentioned being asked for a list of trucks and your exact answer at page 12969, lines 10 to 12, was you said there were six or seven trucks. All this was never mentioned to you even in your Sunday interview with the Prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the conversation involving those names that I've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the fact, Mr. Acimovic, that on the same page at lines 12 to 14, you mentioned for the first time that Popovic had asked you to call the drivers to come to the school, that was the first time that you mentioned this also, two days ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was quite clear. If that question had been asked before, I would have mentioned those people's names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your testimony on the same page, at lines 16 and 19, you mentioned for the first time that you pretended to make those phone calls but that you did not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I made them but I can't remember what I did at that moment. I was alone at the office because Popovic had left the room, but I know that I did not contact with those soldiers. I cannot recall the exact course of my actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Acimovic, I will recall you the exact words you used two days ago and I will read those to you. Lines 16 to 19. Or 15 to 19. And you said, "I picked up the phone. He left the office again, and I dialed the numbers. Now, I can't remember the details why I wasn't able to get in touch with those persons." And then you said, "I know that I played some tricks in order not to be able to get in touch with those drivers, not to be able to call them, and in the end I did not call any of the drivers." It appears to me, Mr. Acimovic, that what you were saying there is that you don't recall why you were not able to reach the drivers. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I never had the intention to contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you're changing your testimony now and saying that if had you wanted to call them you would have been able to do so? Is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I made that call or not, I don't remember, but I pretended, made believe, that those people were not there, so I answered Popovic that there were no drivers around, but I cannot exactly remember in which sequence events unfolded and what specifically I did at that moment. I don't remember if I said the drivers were on home leave or were temporarily absent. I can't tell you that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it is your testimony, and you maintain the fact that maybe you made the call as you just said but you did not reach anyone. Is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get in touch with any of the drivers, because I never meant to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, one quick question concerning something you said yesterday for the first time. You said that you had -- and I will quote. It's on pages 16, lines 1 to 5, yesterday, and you said the following: "I shouted after him, 'I'm not going to wait. I'm going to leave before.'" You also said, "However he went down the corridor. Whether he left the school or whether he stayed on I'm not sure. A few moments later or maybe a few minutes later, I decided to leave that place where I was." Now, I put it to you, Mr. Acimovic, that it's the first time that you indicate having the courage to say anything to Popovic during all the time that you were in the Rocevic school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever mention before, Mr. Acimovic, shouting after Popovic and saying, "I'm not going to wait. I'm going to leave before"? Did you ever mention this before yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him specifically more than ten times that day that I was not going to wait for that person who was supposed to be coming to Rocevic, that I would go back to my unit instead without waiting for that person. I don't know exactly how many times but I told Popovic more than once, several times certainly, that I'm going back to my unit and that I'm not going to wait for that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we have the witness take his headphones off?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls? In private session or in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would just refer my friend to the second interview, page 31, in case he wants to make any corrections to his assertion that the witness had never discussed leaving before and had never said anything to Popovic about it. At lines 16-23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt my colleague but that's a matter for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it's not a matter for re-examination, excuse me, if the transcript is misstated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being suggested to you that you are putting something which is -- putting to the witness a statement that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The gist of what I'm saying Mr. President is that the witness never said before that he shouted at Popovic, "I'm not going to wait, I'm going to leave." He never said he shouted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that was not very clear as the point. What I saw as the point was that he has never said that he was going to leave and that's exactly what he says in the transcript. Just without the word "shout".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But now it's clear I think that the point is that he shouted rather than just stated. Yes. And I suggest that you rephrase your question and specify to the witness that what you're referring to is the characteristic of shouting rather than just stating or uttering something. So that we make sure that the witness is fine-tuned together with the two of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, just to make my question clear, I'll ask my question again. What I was saying a little earlier is that yesterday you mentioned for the first time that you shouted at Popovic, and that you had never mentioned this before. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I mentioned several times that I had told him that I was not going to wait for whoever was coming, that instead I was going back to my unit. And as far as I know, I said that in my previous statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me move on, Mr. Acimovic. I was referring to the word "shouted", but let's move on to something else. I refer now to the transcript of 20th of June two days ago, page 58, lines 7 to 8, as well as page 54, lines 14 to 16. And on those two places, you stated that Popovic had been coming in and leaving the office. Now, it appears to me, Mr. Acimovic, that you had quite a few opportunities to leave the school in Rocevic and to extract yourself from the situation but you chose to stay for a period of well over one hour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was coming and going. He left the room briefly in order to come back again, and he never left very far. He was in the corridor, in the hallway. It's not like he was gone for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can we go in private session, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, it is your testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It is your testimony today that Vujo Lazarevic and Mitar Lazarevic were present in the battalion command during the events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's also your testimony that you briefed them at all times concerning what was going on? For example, when you came back to the command the first time, after meeting with the president and the priest, you briefed them of the situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And with regards to what you spoke about concerning the telegram and the response, that they would be aware of this because they were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that they would also be aware of any and how you consulted with the company commanders during that night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose they should have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And they would also know, because they were there, about the second telegram that you received or you say that you say you receive and the response, the second response, you sent to the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. Is it your testimony that the two individuals I'm talking about would be aware of the second telegram that was received and the second response which was sent?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose they should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you would also have informed them and discussed with them the alleged phone calls from Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe they were present when that discussion took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And coming back after your alleged meeting at the Rocevic school, you would also have briefed them as to what was going on there and the preparations for the execution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed them partially. I cannot be sure now but I described in an outline what was going on at Rocevic and then when I came back, trying to get in touch with the brigade command, I explained what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you -- at that point, you mention in your testimony that you made some phone calls to the brigade. So they would also be aware of those phone calls that you made to the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I believe they should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. I mentioned Vujo Lazarevic and Mitar Lazarevic because I remember them. But it's possible that there were some more members of the command or those who were at the command were there all the time but I can't remember them now. The investigation will establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Acimovic, we have lots of information, both in this trial and that was given to us by the Prosecution, that the prisoners would have arrived in Rocevic on the 14th of June -- 14th of July, sorry. Would you agree with this date? Because you told me -- you said that you did not remember the date but would you agree that this is the date that you met with the priest and the local president?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an approximate time. I cannot be quite certain that it was the 14th. In one of my statements, I did not give the date because I said I didn't remember, but it was in mid-July.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me make that easier for you. If it is established that the prisoners did arrive on the 14th, that's the same day that you saw them or that you saw the school with the president and the priest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a different topic, and that is concerning the sending of telegrams. And I would like you to explain -- first of all, confirm that there are no machines of any type at the battalion command where you can receive a telegram in writing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In fact, the telegram is an oral communication by telephone or by radio; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And a telegram has an official character, either because it's an order or it carries some information that is important to the battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And usually the persons who have authority to issue orders will send a telegram, or the duty officer on their behalf; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what is the procedure at the battalion level when a telegram is received? Because we discussed communications earlier. When the call is received by the radio operator, is he the one to write down the telegram or will he connect the call to the battalion command so that the duty officer can write it down? Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he passes it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So using the switchboard, he plugs it to the battalion command and it is the duty officer who will write down the contents of the telegram; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question with certainty because sometimes it's possible for a soldier to note down the whole telegram and then forward it to the battalion command, the person who is in the signals unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I don't know. I wasn't there. So are you saying that it's possible that the radio operator wrote down the telegram that night?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that he wrote it down or passed it on. I'm not sure. I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What was normal procedure for telegrams? The radio operator would note it or the duty officer? Because they are not sitting in the same room so I'd like to know which one of the two is noting down the telegram.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's forwarded, then the duty officer notes it down. If it's a short telegram, the person notes it down on their own paper and then passes it on to the duty officer at the battalion command. I suppose that is the way they did it. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you receive a telegram that contains instructions or an order, there is a format when a telegram is sent or communicated in an oral conversation, and would you agree with me that it begins by who the telegram is from, the sending unit, there is a "to" section which is the addressee. There is a title which says order or report, there is the contents of telegram and there is the signing authority or on whose behalf the telegram is issued. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. That's probably the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you are sending a telegram from the battalion, the reverse procedure applies, so who drafts the telegram?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The telegram is noted by the duty officer at the battalion command. In fact, he transmits what I told him, if I am the person concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then, does he take the paper over to the radio operator or does he simply get connected and he himself passes on the telegram over the military secure line?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he personally transmits the telegram over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And is this what happened that night?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think the duty officer passed the telegram on to the signals unit, and the signals unit on to the brigade. I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what about the coding of telegrams? How does that work? Can you explain to us how does it work when you want to code a telegram?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said there was a table for encryption of telegrams, and this table was at the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He gave this information yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have lots of questions on telegrams, lots of questions on coding so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try not to ask him questions that he has already answered. I mean, move to your question but avoid repetitions, please, because you put a question that has already been put, he gives you an answer that he has already given and we go on and on and on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, he has not explained how you code a telegram and I would like to know how he uses that book that he's talking about, what's in that book. I would like him to explain exactly what is in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then ask him that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What is in that book, Mr. Acimovic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a table that is in the possession of every unit and it is used when the brigade commander, or somebody else who is in authority, deems it necessary that the telegram should be encrypted, encoded. So if it's an encrypted telegram, it means that it's strictly confidential, that a minimal number of people is aware of the telegram. I suppose that's what you want to hear.
