utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how does the coded telegram look like? If I look at it do I see words? Do I see numbers? Do I see sentences or do I see symbols?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a combination of all of those, numbers, words, depends on the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who is able to decode a telegram? Let me be more precise. Who will decode a telegram at the battalion command? Is it the radio operator in the signals section or is it the duty officer in the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you last time I cannot tell you with any certainty who decoded those telegrams. They were already decoded by the time I was woken up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And there are, I put it to you, Mr. Acimovic, there is more than one book that can be used for coding a telegram. There is actually a book with sentences and a book with numbers. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a question you should ask of a qualified person, a technical person who is qualified about communications. I told you I'm not qualified to give you such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you telling today, Mr. Acimovic, that you could not decode a telegram in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you saying no, you cannot or no, you could? Could you in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that every officer on duty should be able to decode a telegram. Should.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how many books do they use, two books like I say, or one book like you say?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you ever recall coding yourself a telegram where every letter was replaced by a number?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I had no occasion to send or receive encoded telegrams because the communications we had were such that we did not mean -- need to send such telegrams, because we were static, we stayed within our unit. In my opinion, encoded telegrams were used to communicate with units somewhere out in the field where they did not have such means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that the purpose of coding a telegram is to avoid interception; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you have a secure line, which cannot be intercepted, there is no need to use codes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a question I cannot answer because I am not the one who decided how that telegram would be sent to my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And why would anyone in your opinion, as someone who was there at the time, why would anyone use an unsecure line to communicate sensitive information without using codes, if you have a secure line to do so?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot answer your question because it's not clear to me at all. You're asking me as if I had been the one sending the telegram. I cannot guess what was in that person's mind. But I would advise you to consult with your client, the person you are representing, and he will give you precise information about all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, that's not the issue right now that we are dealing with. We are simply dealing with -- I'm asking you if you have a choice between a secure line and a line that is unsecure, and you have sensitive information to convey, you will use the secure line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was emphasised that we should respond to the telegram in the same way the telegram was sent to us. I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's another new information that comes out today for the first time; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which information?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The fact that there was a mention on that telegram that you were to reply by the same means. I've never heard that before, unless you can correct me.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard that before either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I suggest to you, Mr. Acimovic, that coding was never used to transmit telegrams between the brigade and the battalions using a secured line. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what you are suggesting. Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, I will repeat, Mr. Acimovic. I suggest to you that telegrams sent between the brigade and the battalions were never coded because they were transmitted using a secure line.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in my previous answer I told you the same thing that you are telling me now. It was not the practice to send coded telegrams if we were in our own area of defence and if we had the means of communication I described. In all likelihood, but this is my assumption, in all likelihood the person who sent this wanted to protect some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, I made reference earlier on to coding a message where each letter is replaced by a number. Do you recall and can you confirm that these numbers were changed at regular intervals?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those tables must have been changed for security reasons from time to time. I believe every 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that opens up the possibility for mistakes if the duty officer does not use the right table; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I'll try to answer your questions as briefly as possible because I believe they have no relevance at all. From all I can see, I think you're trying to keep me here in the courtroom as long as possible asking me senseless questions, and I'm sorry for taking this liberty to say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was thinking a few minutes ago that you were showing signs of tiredness. I think after having been a Judge and a lawyer for so long, I can have a good feeling of this. So I'm taking that into consideration. Yesterday I told you, please, not to use language that shouldn't be used. I mean, telling Mr. Bourgon, "You're asking me senseless questions," is not something that we can tolerate. So you will soon be out of here. We'll have a break soon. I think perhaps we can anticipate the break and have it now, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If that pleases the Court, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With your indulgence, but please do consider you too what I have just been saying. I can see signs of tiredness in the witness, and it doesn't benefit anyone. I know that you also have all this thrown on you and that's no fun for you either and that it must be tiring for you too but the thing is I just want to make sure that everyone is feeling at ease as much as possible. So we'll have a 25-minute break. And if the witness needs more, then we'll give him some more time. Please try to not to get overexcited. Calm down. As I said yesterday, there will be questions; you need to answer them. If you can answer them, you answer them. If you can't, don't answer them. How much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have four more areas to go into, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we ready to go? Mr. Acimovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, I didn't even need a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, let's get back into quickly in the telegram business, and you trying to call the brigade that night. You mentioned that that evening you contacted the brigade duty officer twice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's once from Kozluk and once when you arrive at the battalion command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it that when you did call the brigade, which connection did you ask for? I take it you asked for the duty officer connection.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't I answer this question a thousand times?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No. It was never put to you, Mr. Acimovic, which connection you asked for when you picked up the phone to call the brigade.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that you like me a lot, you want to keep me in this courtroom and look at me for another week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move. There is a difference between which connections you spoke to and which connection you asked for. And the question is which connection you asked for, if you asked for one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke to the duty officer and asked for the Chief of Staff or the commander, if the commander had shown up in the meantime. Or anyone else with whom I could talk at that moment about the events that we are talking about. I insisted on that. I asked if by any chance any of the other officers were present so I could talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe it's my question that was not clear enough. We established today when I asked you questions that there is a switchboard at the brigade command and when you called the switchboard, you asked which office you want. I'd like you to confirm that you did ask for the office of the duty officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why we have signalsmen, so that all these formalities can be done beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And once you were with the office of the duty officer, you mentioned during your testimony that you did not remember who was the duty officer but that you might have known at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably knew at the time when I was talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you forgot since then?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that's the least of our problems. I think it's very easy to find out who was on duty that night or to establish the identity of the duty officer's deputy or assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: May we go into private session, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you want me to repeat the question again? The morning that you say you went to Rocevic, the day you went in the school, you said that you called the brigade to try and get ahold of the commander or the Chief of Staff and you were told they were not available; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we have information, Mr. Acimovic, that on that day, both the commander and the Chief of Staff were present in the headquarters. On this basis I suggest to you that because there's no message in the logbook and because that those persons were in the headquarters, again you did not call that day to speak to the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you say. What you're saying is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Sorry for that. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just think it might be helpful if my friend would say what he means by "the commander and the Chief of Staff were there that day." Does he mean the whole day or what part of the day? I don't know what he's putting to the witness exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: M'hm. Yes. I think that's a pertinent remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can make my the next addition to that but I remember the witness mentioned he tried to get in touch with commander possibly when he returned to the -- his battalion but he didn't mention about the commander in the morning time but I would leave it to the Defence of Mr. Pandurevic so I will not pursue this one further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Judge and Mr. President, I'm trying to cut down as much as I can on my cross-examination, and I thought I could join those two events in the morning, the phone call before he went to Rocevic and the phone call when he came back from Rocevic from his battalion command but those are two different instances. Now what I'm saying is that he did call on those two occasions and I'm suggesting to him that he did not call on the basis that either on one or two of these occasions those people were present and they would have taken the call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There is no way that can be clear to the witness from the way he's just put it unless he gives the timeframes he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have to give precise times. Divide it into two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will be easier. Judge Kwon? It's okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, when you say that you called the brigade command in the morning, I suggest to you that either the commander or the Chief of Staff were present and that either of them would have taken your call and that shows that you did not call in the morning. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I still think this is kind an important. It's a bit vague. When in the morning is he talking about and suggesting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I think now we are really wasting time because my colleague knows exactly that this is just before he left to go to Rocevic and I think everybody knows that and that now we are really wasting time and I think the witness knows that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear. Let's get the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Before you left for Rocevic in the morning, you said you made a phone call to the brigade. I'm saying there was no phone call on the basis that there was one of the two individuals you were looking for to take your call. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're saying is not true. I called the brigade and asked for these persons and I was told that they were not there. I don't know how many times I've said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you returned from Rocevic, from your battalion command, you called again and you requested to speak to either the commander or the Chief of Staff and again I'm saying that this call was never placed, because one of these two individuals, as a minimum, was there and they would have taken your call. And I'm suggesting to you that you did not call on that occasion. Is that correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you did say both in your testimony and in your interviews that when you called the second time, that is after you returned from Rocevic, you would agree with me that this was around 12.00 on that second day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was between 11.30 and 12.15. It was sometime in that interval.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did say, did you not, Mr. Acimovic, that you spoke to the duty officer who was -- who by that time had changed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer had probably changed by that time, but I cannot say with any certainty. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'm putting it to you, Mr. Acimovic, because there is no trace in the operative duty officer's notebook of any phone call made by you, that you did not make that second call that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I further suggest to you that when you called, you did not speak to Drago Nikolic when you came back from Rocevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which day you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you came back from Rocevic the second day, we are talking about the same phone call that you say you made, between 11.30 and 12.15, that you did not speak to Drago Nikolic on that occasion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even say that I had spoken to Drago Nikolic that day. I spoke to him the previous night.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's what I'm saying, Mr. Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Mr. Acimovic, I'm telling you that Drago Nikolic was the duty officer during the time frame that you say you called, that you did not speak to him, and that in fact you never called the brigade and never made that second call. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move on to -- just to go back quickly to the consultation which took place with the company commanders. That is what you say when you received that first telegram. First, let me confirm that you -- it is your testimony that the first telegram was sent to the company commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that telegram was passed on to company commanders as well or maybe it was the second telegram, but I believe that company commanders found out about the orders only after the second telegram, because it seems to me, and I've said so last time, that the telegram said, among other things, "Notify company commanders."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the second telegram, pursuant to your testimony, required you to get in touch personally with the company commanders and that's what you did; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this consultation took place by phone, and your main purpose was to ensure that if somebody would ask them if you had consulted with them, they were in a position to say yes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that, but to consult with them about the contents of the telegram, to explain to them what it was all about. And having done that, we jointly came to the conclusion that it was somebody's lunatic idea and that we have no men to give for that purpose, and I never looked for any.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the sense of those -- that consultation with the company commanders -- strike that, Mr. President. I'll move on to another topic. Yes. Just one question in relation to this. That communication was also made using the military phone or the secure line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to a different topic, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are we in private session? I think we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session but we'll go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'll just ask, I take it that my friend is not willing and doesn't wish to share any of these reports with us which he's received. And that we rely then just on his interpretation of them and that he's getting them as accurately as he has Dragan Jokic's testimony and other references he's made to the transcript and to prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I can go one by one and I can get -- provide further details but then I'm trying to cut down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is information I'll bring forward in the Defence case, or it will be led before in the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you deal with it directly with Mr. Nicholls after the sitting. Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to repeat your question because we will have to go back to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Without the names, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the basis, Mr. Acimovic, of all the information I told you we have collected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, you had -- this is what we have in our transcript anyway. To the question put to you by Mr. Bourgon you said, "I can't be burdened by your claims and I tell you once again that this is simply not correct." Was that your full answer or before we interrupted you or at the time we interrupted or did you mean to give more information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Your next question, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, I -- on the basis of the information or the names of the people we collected information from, I suggest to you that there was never an order or a request sent to your battalion to put together a platoon of soldiers to participate in the -- in any executions. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. What I'm saying is that you are not telling the truth. That's the least I can tell you. And the same applies to your previous questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, just so that we make things clear. It's not me that's not telling the truth. I'm referring to information that I have obtained. I'm just an advocate representing his clients in this case and I put it to you that there were never a coded message that made its way to your battalion concerning the execution of prisoners in Rocevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your claim. I'm absolutely not interested in your claims or your assumptions. So much from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, all I need from you is to either deny or say that you agree with my suggestion. That's all I'm asking of you and that information will make its way into this trial. And then the Judges will decide. There was nobody trained in your communications section, in your battalion, to code or decode telegrams; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. In your battalion, the 2nd Battalion, there was, amongst your communication staff, your signalman or your radio operator - with translation it can sometimes be difficult - there was nobody who was trained who could code and decode messages and there was no book of codes in the communications section. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every signalsman has been trained to decipher any message that arrives in the unit. They were trained to decipher every order, every task, every message. That was their duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, I suggest to you that the information that you obtained concerning persons being detained in Rocevic school was provided to you by someone who travelled to your battalion and provided you with this information and it is not something that you found out yourself on the 14th of July with the priest and the president, as you say. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, I suggest to you that there are three other battalions who received information and instructions concerning prisoners being held in schools, the 4th Battalion, the 1st Battalion, and the 6th Battalion. In every case, there was never any request to provide anyone to participate in executions, and I put it to you that if you receive any information from the brigade, it did not include any request to send people to participate in executions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a compound question. Let's divide it into two parts, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And why are you standing up, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because I don't think that what has been put to the witness is accurate and if we want to go into it, he'll have to take his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Mr. Acimovic, can I ask to you remove your headphones again, please? The question was premised on Mr. Bourgon's stating that he has information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it would be accurate to say that the 4th Battalion, Lazar Ristic's men, did receive requests and instructions to participate in executions. So it's not fair to say that no other battalion received any of this type of information or instructions concerning prisoners held in schools.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm doing my best to finish as quickly as possible so my colleague can do his re-exam and we can send the witness home. I was talking about battalion and I'm talking, of course, battalion commands, battalion commands and my colleague understood that question. I'm simply suggesting that the 4th, the 1st and the 6th Battalion, if those command they never received any instructions to provide people to participate in execution, and I'm suggesting to the witness that any information his battalion received was also not related to any executions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think that's clear from the question. It's not just that he's talking about just the command. It's broader than that which is why I made my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to clear that up with the witness first and then we can proceed. But it wasn't clear in my mind either. So I think it needs to be cleared up with the witness first and foremost. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, I'm suggesting to you, and I have to take my question over again, the 4th Battalion command, the 1st Battalion command, and the 6th Battalion command, the three of them received information in relation to prisoners being held in schools but that none of them received information asking them to take part in executions. On this basis --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My colleague all he wants to do is make sure the witness stays for Monday, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's try to avoid such comments, Mr. Bourgon. I mean, we would like the witness to go home too. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again do you want him to remove the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Acimovic, if you can remove your headphones again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't wish to interrupt or slow things down but our position is that the 4th Battalion commander Lazar Ristic received information from his men that they had been requested to participate in executions. So the way he's phrased the question is that none of these commands received information of these requests and that's just not accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There seems to be a disagreement on you on whether the command had received so I think that can become a matter for re-examination -- for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I see you both standing still. Yes Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't intend to re-examine on it and I wouldn't be surprised if the witness wasn't able to answer about what information -- I just want the questions to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we were talking about, too. Mr. Bourgon, it's being put to you that the proposition to the witness that the 4th command -- Battalion command never received such instructions is not a correct one. What your position on that? Before we put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My position is that the 4th Battalion did not receive a request to send anyone to participate in executions and there is a disagreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then put the question, let him answer, and we'll see where it takes us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, I'm doing my best to finish with you today so that we can send you back home. Your battalion, I'm putting, I'm suggesting to you, and that's what I'm suggesting, that your battalion did not receive any instructions -- strike that. Do you know, Mr. Acimovic, that there is a 1st Battalion, a 6th Battalion and a 4th Battalion in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm telling you -- I'm suggesting to you that these battalions did not receive any request to send soldiers to participate in the execution of any prisoners. And I'm suggesting to you that the same goes for your battalion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to talk about any other units. I don't want to enter into that debate. Please ask me questions about my units only. As for the other infantry battalions, I have no information that I could share with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have no more questions for you, Mr. Acimovic. Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes? Let's -- Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, no, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I have specific instructions that I'm not to be the cause of this witness remaining here over the weekend but there is just -- there are just one or two questions I would like to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt I'm not sure -- I think my friend might have done that in private session and he may have reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think Mr. Nicholls is right. We did have it in private session so let's redact and move to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The presence of these prisoners in the school at Rocevic was a complete surprise to you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when you first saw these prisoners, they were already in the school at Rocevic, in the gym of the school at Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you had nothing to do with opening up the gym of the school for those prisoners to be put inside, did you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have anything whatsoever to do with the bringing of these prisoners of war in the gym, and I had no contact with them at all, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I simply wanted to clarify that because in answer to Mr. Bourgon's question you admitted the possibility that you might have got the keys to the offices of the school. That presumably, if it was possible, was it sometime later, after the prisoners were already in there?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me? I apologise. I'm afraid I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's all right. I'm not going to ask it again. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, you had indicated you had a few questions. Do you think you can finish in seven minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't want to waste time. I object to the questions being asked again. I think the only basis is the log I used. That was nothing new. That had been disclosed a long time ago. It wasn't on our list but I think he had ample time to prepare to ask questions on that vehicle log which was used during my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear what your question is and we'll decide whether to allow to you go ahead or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you with your leave, Your Honours, yesterday we received information that the document would be used by the Prosecution in their examination-in-chief. This was done after your suggestion during the examination-in-chief of this witness when he could not remember the family name of a person of whom he was talking, and it was only then that we received the document from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, I'll try and be very brief. I'm putting again in the context that I laid for you yesterday, I'm contesting the fact that my client was ever in contact with the people of whom you spoke, that he was ever in contact with you. Could you please look at this document, this is 225, and I believe that we should move into private session. This is Prosecution Exhibit number 295.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I can confirm that the Prosecution doesn't have any re-examination. Yes, we'll do the tendering next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, sorry I said no re-examination. I did want to just ask the witness he said look here, he wanted to point at something. I think he might have gotten cut off. If he wanted to mention something else about the document, I'd like him to have the chance to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there anything else you wish to add before we send you home, Mr. Acimovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing in particular. I just wanted to ask whether the car was the Mercedes or the TAM 2000. I believe that the vehicle in question was the TAM 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll look into that anyway. Mr. Acimovic, I wish to thank you for having come over on behalf of the Trial Chamber and I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We stand adjourned until Monday -- do you wish to ask something?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, very quickly. Our deadline to submit our papers on the intercepts is this Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I must say, Mr. President, that I am running late and I did not have time to finish and I'm not sure I'll be able to finish by Monday. And I would like to have an extension. I don't know if that applies to my other colleagues or not but I would like to have an extension, Mr. President, a short extension, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a guillotine in Quebec?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My only comment, which I had mentioned to

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is there any point any of us submitting anything until this joinder matter is decided upon? If General Tolimir joins this case, I imagine he might have something to say about the matter. Perhaps Your Honours will ponder that over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I ask rhetorically, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to know first what Mr. Tolimir thinks all about this. Let's adjourn, and we'll deal with this later on Monday. But for the time being take it that there will be an extension in any case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of June 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
